Notes: Year Established basis: earliest datable evidence of Jewish presence at Khirbet Qana is Hasmonean coinage (Hasmonean period 140-37 BCE, midpoint -90 per convention). The article states that Hasmonean coins found at the site indicate 'Maccabean influence by the 1st century BC', though no Hasmonean-period buildings have been identified. It also says coins and Jewish-script ostraca point to a predominantly Jewish population in the Hellenistic and Roman periods. Some popular reports (Aleteia 2018, Archaeology Magazine 2025) describe Khirbet Qana as a Jewish village from 323 BCE; that is a period bracket (Hellenistic-Roman), not dated evidence, so it is not used for Year Established. No population figure.

Khirbet Qana Project (University of Puget Sound) site history: once Hasmonean (Maccabean) Jewish rule extended to Galilee, 'much of Cana probably became Jewish' (Hasmonean annexation of Galilee, c. late 2nd-early 1st c. BCE; year set to the Hasmonean-period midpoint, c.). The same page says the town grew after the first Jewish revolt, possibly with refugees from the fighting around Jerusalem (post-70, not dated). Judaization event; no population figure.

Early Roman period (63 BCE-70 CE; midpoint 4, c.). Schuler (CTQ 71, 2007), summarising Richardson 2006, identifies biblical Cana with Khirbet Qana and describes a planned hillside village: terraced houses following the contours, streets and stepped lanes, and on the north slope larger courtyard houses with storage rooms and 'even a mikveh'. He notes economic differentiation (three house types), kokhim-type (Jewish) tombs, and mechanized oil presses of the Hasmonean and early Roman periods (citing Aviam 2004). This suggests a modest Jewish agricultural village. No population estimate is given.

Public building interpreted as a synagogue (or beth midrash) at Khirbet Qana. McCollough (BAR 41:6, 2015), endnote 4: ceramic evidence from the foundation strata dates its founding to the early Roman period, and C14 dating of foundation mortar gives 4-224 CE (95%). Year set to the early Roman midpoint (4, c.). Evidence of an organized Jewish community; no population figure.

Gospel of John 2:1-11: a wedding 'in Cana of Galilee' during Jesus' ministry (c. 28-30 CE; year c. 30), with 'six stone water jars for the Jewish rites of purification' (2:6). John 4:46 says Jesus returned to Cana, and John 21:2 names Nathanael 'of Cana in Galilee'. This is a literary attestation of a Jewish village. Its identification with Khirbet Qana rather than Kafr Kanna is favoured by many scholars but disputed. No population figure.

Khirbet Qana Project (University of Puget Sound): 'Jewish presence is evident in stone vessels, miqveh, the earliest synagogue in Galilee, and a Jewish amulet'. Also an industrial area with presses and a columbarium, Roman tombs and imported roof tiles and wares. These are undated in the source; the earliest synagogue in Galilee implies the 1st c. CE (midpoint 50, c.). Organized Jewish village community; no population figure. The same page notes a later tradition (after 70 CE) that a priestly course settled there.

Jensen (Biblica 93, 2012): excavations at Cana (Khirbet Qana, citing Edwards 2002) produced 'material evidence of a small village community in a steady process of expansion'. They found two public buildings and small-scale oil, textile and glass production. Dated to the first-century stratum (1st c. CE, midpoint 50, c.). Small village; no population figure.

Josephus, Life 86 (Whiston ch. 16): during the Great Revolt (winter 66/67 CE), Josephus, the Jewish commander of Galilee, says 'my abode was in a village of Galilee, which is named Cana' (spelled 'Cans' in this transcription; Greek Kana). He was in the plain of Asochis (Life 207), which fits Khirbet Qana on the north edge of the Beth Netofa valley. This attests a Jewish village used as the commander's base. No population figure.

Jensen (Biblica 93, 2012) groups Yodefat and Cana as settlements of special interest 'since their destruction during the Jewish War' sealed their first-century stratum (Vespasian's Galilean campaign of 67 CE, c.). Population is left blank: the source does not say that no Jews remained. Other sources (Khirbet Qana Project) say the village continued and grew after the revolt, so the extent of any destruction is uncertain.

BAR caption (Khirbet Qana Project, McCollough 2015): 'Several archaeological discoveries attest to the Jewish identity of Khirbet Cana from the Hellenistic and Roman periods'. The evidence on this caption is several miqva'ot (ritual baths) of the same period as the synagogue building. A companion caption in the same article dates that building to the late 1st or early 2nd c. CE. Year set to c. 70, the end of the period. A three-letter abecedary ostracon in Jewish script, dated late 1st-2nd c. CE, probably falls after the period and has no row. Ritual baths indicate a Jewish residential community; no population figure.
